entries.location: Unit 1 Mechanics: Chapter 1 Units and Measurement: Section 1.6 Significant Figures
entries.additional_location_information: Right after subheader "Significant figures in calculations"
entries.detail:
Book states: "When combining measurements with different degrees of precision, the number of significant digits in the final answer can be no greater than the number of significant digits in the least-precise measured value."
This may be true for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, but it is not true for other common mathematics such as exponentials or trig functions. Consider an uncertainty of ±0.5% (i.e. two significant figures or 1% absolute bound):
• log(98) vs log(99): error of only 0.2%. log() can actually *increase* the number of significant figures. 
• tan(98°) vs tan(99°): error of 11%.
• tan(98rad) vs tan(99rad): error of 3500%. Not even 1 sig fig. 
• 10^98 vs 10^99: error of 900%. Only 1 sig fig.
• 98! vs 99!: error of 9900%. Not even 1 sig fig!
• Sphere radius from surface area r = (3A/(4π))^(1/3), using 98 vs 99: 2.8698/2.8601 or 0.34% error. Only 3rd digit changes. Almost 3 sig figs!

This may seem a minor point, but it matters in places where we frequently take logs or higher exponents, like pH or thermal physics, respectively. 

Suggested resolution: 
"When combining measurements with different degrees of precision, if the only mathematical operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, then the number of significant digits in the final answer can be no greater than the number of significant digits in the least-precise measured value. 
...For other operations such as exp(x) or log(x), the actual uncertainty should be calculated instead of relying only on significant digits.
entries.resolution_notes: Revise the sentence "When combining measurements with..." to "When combining measurements with different degrees of precision with the mathematical operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, then the number of significant digits in the final answer can be no greater than the number of significant digits in the least-precise measured value."

entries.detail:
"It is simply a way of rounding numbers consistently to the nearest power of 10."

The order of magnitude of 450 is 3, since 4.5 > 10^0.5 and 450  = 4.5 x 10^2, or log(450)=2.65 which rounds up to 3. The closest power of 10 is 100, which is 350 units away compared to 550 units to 1000. Therefore, computing the order of magnitude in this regard does not round consistently to the nearest power of 10 as stated in the text, but still provides a means to reason about the scale of numbers in a general way.
entries.resolution_notes: Revise "to the nearest power of 10." to "to the nearest (on a logarithmic scale) power of 10. In other words, if numbers differ by one order of magnitude, the one is larger than the other by about ten."

entries.location: Chapter 2: Vectors, Section: Products of Vectors
entries.detail:
It turns out that there is no universally agreed upon definition of the term "lever arm".  It would be nice if the authors of this textbook would settle on a definition and use it consistently.  Unfortunately, that did not happen.

In the chapter on vectors the lever arm is defined as the vector from the axle to the point of application of the force. Note: this version of the lever arm is a vector.  In the chapter in which torques are defined, the lever arm is re-defined as the perpendicular distance from the axle to the line of action of the force. Note: this is not a vector, and it is smaller in magnitude than the vector defined in the earlier part of the book by a factor of sin\theta.

I'm betting that there are multiple choice questions students see which will assume one of these definitions.  Consistency in the definition of lever arm would be most welcome.   Graeme Dewar, University of North Dakota

"Even in everyday life we naturally invoke the concept of orthogonal projections in a rectangular coordinate system. For example, if you ask someone for directions to a particular location, you will more likely be told to go 40 km east and 30 km north than 50 km in the direction  37°  north of east."

This is apparently the only definition of orthogonal projection presented in the text.

Clearly the author knows what it is but a new reader might not.

". In the Cartesian system, the x and y vector components of a vector are the orthogonal projections of this vector onto the x- and y-axes, respectively. In this way, following the parallelogram rule for vector addition, each vector on a Cartesian plane can be expressed as the vector sum of its vector components:"

The definition of vector components as  orthogonal projections adds needless jargon.  "projection" is basically an undefined term in which the reader is meant to infer that 30 km North and 40 km East are projections from the previous paragraph.

There seems to be no further clarification of "projection" when it later comes up more appropriately in vector multiplication.

I would propose to completely remove the problem, or fully reword so as to explicitly state the presumption being made in the solution. The solution to the problem, as given, has mistakes, but it can be reconstructed if one presumes that both aircraft have been continuously moving away from the tower along a straight-line path with the tower as their common origin, so their velocity and position vectors are colinear (which isn't generally true). However, such an assumption/presumption is not justified in general as all vectors are invariant under translation. The minimal information given is valid independent of the airport tower, but one aircraft could be, say from JFK and the other from LGA: the minimal information may still be accurate, but the presumption that they started climbing from the same airport (tower) is wrong. The only way to make the minimal information provided sufficient for a valid and unambiguous solution is to explicitly state that both aircraft can be presumed to be moving (velocity) continuously in a straight line with their common take-off origin being the base (ground level) of the tower.

entries.detail:
Question itself is stated ambiguously; it asks to "Compare the distance traveled of an object ... with an object ..." and never says whether these two objects had the same initial velocity. Suggest modifying "... over the same time period" to say "... over the same time period starting with the same initial velocity."

*ASSUMING* the same initial velocity (which reasonable problem-solvers could assume), the given solution has mistakes in it. Solution says x1 = (3/2)*v0*t, and that's wrong. Initial velocity was v0, change in initial velocity was 2v0, so the final velocity was 3v0. Then according to average velocity (const. acceleration) formula, the average velocity is v_avg = (v0 + 3v0)/2 = 4v0/2, not 3v0/2, yielding x1 (multiplying by duration of time for displacement) equal to (4/2)*v0*t (or 2v0*t). x2, similarly, should be (6/2)*v0*t or (6/4)*x1 = (3/2)*x1. Original answer key might have been calculated with the mistake that either treated initial velocity as 0 (in average velocity formula) or mis-interpreted "undergoes a change in velocity that is twice its initial velocity" as saying "obtains a final velocity that is double its initial velocity". Either way, either the answer key should be corrected or the problem re-worded (in addition to clarifying that initial velocity in two cases are same) so that the answer key matches the problem as written.
entries.resolution_notes: Our reviewers accepted this change, and the question will be updated in the next print cycle.

This comes from the definition of average speed as circumference divided by the time it takes to go in a circle:

v = 2πr/T

This problem has already been revised once. The new version, visible online Fall 2020, reads:

"A team of nine members on a tall building tug on a string attached to a large boulder on an icy surface. The boulder has a mass of 200 kg and is tugged with a force of 2350 N. (a) What is magnitude of the acceleration? (b) What force would be required to produce a constant velocity?" 

The suggested solution to this problem, indicated in Errata revision 9847, is: "Revise the answer to: a. 1.95 m/s^2 b. 1960 N"

It is unclear why nine members (of what group?) are involved in this problem, and what the height of the building is, which is presumably some height above an icy surface. Is the force applied along the angle of the rope (in which case we need to know the height or angle of the rope to identify the horizontal component of Force applied)? The "icy surface" implies a surface of negligible friction, in which case there is no way a force applied can produce a constant velocity.

The previous tug-of-war problem had some issues, easily fixed by specifying a force of friction for each team. Consider restoring that problem as follows:

"Two teams of nine members each engage in a tug-of-war, pulling in opposite directions on a horizontal rope. Each of the first team’s members has an average mass of 68 kg and exerts an average force of 1350 N horizontally on the ground as they pull on the rope. Each of the second team’s members has an average mass of 73 kg and exerts an average force of 1365 N horizontally on the ground as they pull on the rope in the opposite direction. (a) What is magnitude of the acceleration of the two teams, and which team wins? (b) What is the tension in the section of rope between the teams?

Answers: (a) 0.106 m/s^2 in the direction of team 2. Team 2 wins the tug-of-war. (b) Tension = 1.22 x 10^4 N.
entries.resolution_notes:

entries.detail: These equations should not be boxed or numbered. They are not fundamental and are often incorrect (that is, they apply only to limited situations). Equation numbers in the rest of the book seem to be limited to fundamental statements (e.g. F = ma, w = mg). By applying equation numbers and highlighting with boxes, students may perceive these 4 equations as equally fundamental. This is especially problematic with the normal and tension forces, which are a source of wide-spread misconceptions, such as those given in these equations (e.g. N = mg).
entries.resolution_notes: The formatting on these equations will be updated.

entries.additional_location_information: In the section "Weight and Gravitational Force"
entries.detail:
The book currently states, "Weight varies dramatically if we leave Earth’s surface. On the Moon, for example, acceleration due to gravity is only 1.67 m/s^2. A 1.0-kg mass thus has a weight of 9.8 N on Earth and only about 1.7 N on the Moon."

However, this value of 1.67 m/s^2 is not accurate.  On the lunar surface, g is 1.625 m/s^2 (1.63 m/s^2 to 2 sig figs).  Therefore, the 1.0-km mass would have a weight of 1.6 N on the Moon rather than 1.7 N.  

Please fix the value of g_Moon and the weight of the mass on the Moon.
